name: Kollur Mookambika Temple
deity: The Goddess as Mookambika, uniting Shakti with Shiva
period: Ancient shrine, developed through the medieval period
dynasty: Local chiefs and the Keladi Nayakas
summary: At the foot of the Kodachadri hill in coastal Karnataka, Kollur Mookambika is a great goddess shrine where Devi is worshipped as the union of Shiva and Shakti, revered above all as the giver of learning and traditionally linked to Adi Shankara.

sections.history: Kollur lies in the Western Ghats above the Karnataka coast, on the Souparnika river below the peak of Kodachadri. The Mookambika shrine is ancient in tradition and was developed through the medieval centuries under local chiefs and the Keladi Nayakas. It is bound above all to Adi Shankara, the eighth-century teacher, who is said to have installed the goddess here in the form in which she is worshipped. Over the centuries Kollur grew into one of the foremost goddess pilgrimages of the west coast, drawing devotees from Karnataka, Kerala, and far beyond.
sections.architecture: The temple, in the Tulu-Kerala manner of the coast blended with Dravidian forms, enshrines the goddess before a distinctive jyotirlinga marked by a golden line, the svarna-rekha, which divides it into halves sacred to Shiva and to Shakti — so that the two are worshipped as one. A golden-roofed sanctum, pillared halls, and shrines to attendant deities cluster within, and the river Souparnika runs close by for the pilgrims’ ritual bath. Above the temple rises Kodachadri, its forested peak part of the sacred landscape.
sections.legends: The goddess takes her name from the demon Mookasura, whom she slew after he had been struck dumb — mooka — by the gods; as Mookambika she embodies the united power of Kali, Lakshmi, and Saraswati. Tradition holds that Adi Shankara, meditating on Kodachadri, was granted a vision of the Devi and asked her to come with him to a place he would consecrate; she agreed on condition he not look back, and when he did, at Kollur, she stayed, and here he installed her. The golden line on the linga marks this union of Shiva and the Mother.
sections.festivals: Navaratri is Kollur’s greatest festival, the nine nights of the goddess kept with special splendour, and Vidyarambha on Vijayadashami draws families who bring young children to begin their learning at the Devi’s feet, tracing the first letters in her presence. Rathotsava, the car festival, and the annual renewal festivals fill the temple through the year, and as the goddess of Saraswati’s wisdom, Mookambika receives students and scholars seeking her blessing on their studies.
sections.experience: Set in green hill country, Kollur offers a pilgrimage of cool river, forested slopes, and the quiet authority of the goddess. Pilgrims bathe in the Souparnika, then enter to stand before the linga with its golden line, where Shiva and Shakti are one. The Vidyarambha rite, tiny fingers guided to write the first letters in rice, is among the most touching sights in any Indian temple. Beyond the shrine, the peak of Kodachadri calls the more adventurous upward, and the whole valley keeps the fresh, unhurried air of the Ghats.

visit.timings: Generally open from around 5:00 am to 9:00 pm daily with several pujas; hours extend during Navaratri and other festivals.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is removed at the temple.
visit.photography: Photography is generally not permitted inside the sanctum; follow posted rules and staff guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Kollur is in Udupi district, about 80 km from Udupi and Mangaluru, the latter with the nearest airport; the nearest railheads are Kundapura and Byndoor, and the temple is reached by road through the Ghats.
